newsitem.title: USA: UAL pilots reject wage proposal.
newsitem.headline: UAL pilots reject wage proposal.

text.p: Pilots at UAL Corp's United airlines rejected a wage proposal that called for a 10 percent pay increase over four years, the Air Line Pilots Association said Thursday.
The pilots union said 80 percent of its members voted against the wage offer, with 89.4 percent of eligible pilots casting votes.
The rejection marks continued labor unrest in the airline industry, following a bitter dispute between AMR Corp's American Airlines and its pilots.
American and the pilots turned down binding arbitration and entered a 30-day "cooling off" period that could result in a strike or a lockout on February 15.
United Airlines could not be immediately reached to comment on the pilot vote.

"This is not simply a dispute over wages. The pilots' overwhelming rejection of the tentative agreement reflects a vote against a 'business as usual attitude' that has no place in an employee-owned company," said union official Mike Glawe.
The pilots said they "continue to be ready, willing and able to make employee ownership a success at United Airlines."
The vote centered on a wage adjustment which was included as a provision of the pilots July 1994 employee-ownership agreement (ESOP). United's employees own 55 percent of the its common stock.

Now that the wage proposal has been rejected, United and pilots will likely submit to binding arbitration, analysts said. However, some industry experts doubt binding arbitration will smooth the unrest at United.
"This is a horrible turn of events that expresses the depths of the pilots' conflict with United's management," said Joseph Blasi, a professor at Rutgers' School of Management and Labor Relations.
"The company and the workers have to respond to this like an emergency," Blasi said.
A pilot strike is not a concern, however, since United's unions have already agreed not to strike as part of the 1994 ESOP, analysts said.
Labor concerns at United and other U.S. airlines have intensified in recent weeks as carriers boast of record profitability and strong growth.
United's mechanics also rejected a wage increase proposal last week, although ramp, food service, dispatch and other workers accepted the plan.
The labor woes at one carrier oftern lend support to unions at other carriers, analysts said.
"One contract builds on the last. The pilots at the various carriers are going to be watching what happens at American," said Edward Starkman, an analyst with Dillon Read.
"We think the tide has turned and momentum unequivocally favors management," said Bankers Trust analyst Vivian Lee in a recent research report.

Analysts said USAir Group Inc will feel the pressure from the recent pilot movements at United and American. USAir recently presented a proposal to its pilot negotiating committee that calls for wage concessions of about 12 percent, sources said.

"Certainly the industry is reporting much better profits than it has historically and that is making negotiations across the industry more difficult than they would be," AMR Corp's chief financial officer Gerard Arpey said in a recent media teleconference.
"The industry is making good money. But it's a cyclical business and the airlines don't want to give away the store when it's about as good as it's going to get," said Starkman of Dillon Read.
